opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be back.

I think the interesting thing is that science isn't one skill. It's a loop: you form a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, look at the results, and then, crucially, update what you believe and decide what to try next. Current LLMs are very good at pieces of that. They can write code, summarize literature, and draft a paper that reads well. What they struggle with is the connective tissue: noticing that a result is surprising, being honest when an idea didn't work, and choosing the next experiment that's actually informative rather than just plausible.

So when I think about LLMs "learning" science, I don't mean memorizing more papers. I mean learning the process: open-ended search, keeping an archive of ideas that were tried, building on stepping stones that weren't obviously useful at the time. That's very much the open-endedness perspective. Breakthroughs rarely come from optimizing straight toward an objective. They come from accumulating interesting intermediate artifacts and recombining them.

There's also a verification problem we can't ignore. In machine learning research you can at least run the code and get a number, which gives you a grounding signal. But numbers can be gamed. Models will happily find shortcuts, tweak evaluation, or overclaim in the write-up. So part of teaching the scientific process is teaching epistemic hygiene: proper baselines, ablations, multiple seeds, and saying "this didn't replicate." Arguably that's harder than generating ideas.

And then there's taste. Good scientists have a sense of which questions matter and which results are worth chasing. I don't think we've solved how to instill that in a model. Some of it may come from feedback, like reviewer signals or real-world impact over time, and some from scaling the loop itself so the system sees many full research cycles rather than isolated snippets. To me that's the frontier: moving from models that imitate the artifacts of science to systems that actually internalize the iterative, self-correcting process behind them.

r001.rationale: The response describes science as an iterative loop and mentions open-ended search, but it does not frame research as a tree of ideas or experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a paper reports one path through a research search tree.

r003.rationale: It advocates learning from full research cycles, but does not call for training on datasets that capture full research search trees.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the scientific process isn't really one skill, it's a loop. You generate a hypothesis, you design an experiment that could actually falsify it, you run it, you look at the results honestly, and then you update and go again. And most of what we've done with LLMs so far is train them on the artifacts of that loop, the papers, the final clean story, rather than the loop itself.

That's a problem, because papers are the compressed, post-hoc version of science. They don't show the ten experiments that didn't work, the pivot halfway through, the moment where you realized your baseline was broken. So a model that only sees papers learns to write things that sound like science. It learns the form. What it doesn't learn is the taste, the judgment about what's worth trying and when to stop.

So when we built the AI Scientist, a lot of the effort was really about externalizing that loop and making the model actually go through it. It has to write code, run it, read the numbers back, and decide whether the idea held up. And what you see is that the hard part isn't generating ideas. The models are extremely good at producing plausible-sounding hypotheses. The hard part is being skeptical of your own results, noticing when an improvement is noise, noticing when you've accidentally leaked the test set, things like that.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that science is iterative across time, not just within one experiment. Good researchers carry forward a kind of memory of what has been tried, what the failure modes were, and that shapes the next question. For LLM systems that means we need to think about how the system accumulates experience over many cycles, and ideally learns from execution feedback rather than just from human-labeled preferences. Reward from the world, from the experiment actually working, is a much more grounded signal than reward from someone saying the write-up looks nice.

And honestly I think this is where it gets interesting for the field, because once the model is embedded in that loop, the scientific process becomes a training environment. You can measure whether the system is improving at doing science, not just at describing it.

r001.rationale: The response describes science as an iterative loop, but does not conceptualize it as a tree search through ideas or experiments.

r002.rationale: It says papers present a compressed, clean story and omit failed experiments and pivots, conveying that they show only a selected path through the research process.

r003.rationale: It advocates having models execute the scientific loop and learn from feedback, but does not advocate training them on datasets that capture full research search trees.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to think of science as a loop, rather than as producing an answer. You have some observations, you formulate a hypothesis, you design an experiment, and then you update your beliefs based on what actually happens. For an LLM system, the challenge is to learn that whole process, including what to do when an experiment contradicts its initial intuition.

A model can produce a very plausible scientific explanation. But can it propose an experiment that distinguishes between two competing explanations? Can it recognize when the evidence is inconclusive? And can it decide what to investigate next, given a limited budget? Those are much more interesting capabilities to me.

This also makes evaluation difficult, because a failed experiment can be scientifically valuable. You might rule out an entire class of hypotheses. So if you reward only the final successful result, you risk missing the quality of the investigation itself.

I would like to see systems learn through repeated interaction with environments where they can test their ideas and get feedback. The question then becomes whether they develop strategies for discovery that transfer to new problems, beyond the particular experiments they were trained on.

r001.rationale: It describes science as a loop of hypotheses, experiments, and belief updates, but does not conceptualize it as a tree search through ideas or experiments.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss scientific papers or describe them as reporting one path through a research search tree.

r003.rationale: It advocates learning through repeated interaction with environments, but does not advocate training on datasets that capture full research search trees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting part is that science is a process of interacting with something that can tell you you're wrong. You have a hypothesis, you design an experiment, you observe what happens, and then you update your understanding. So the question for an LLM system is whether it can participate in that whole loop, rather than just produce a plausible hypothesis or write up a convincing explanation.

And a lot of the difficulty is deciding what to do next. Which experiment would actually distinguish between two explanations? When should you abandon an idea, and when was the experiment itself poorly designed? A failed experiment can be very informative, but only if you can interpret why it failed.

So I would think about learning the scientific process as learning a policy for discovery. The system needs to choose actions that improve its understanding over time. And then you need environments where you can test that: give it an unfamiliar problem, let it run experiments, and see whether its predictions actually get better. That's a stronger signal than whether its final report sounds scientific.

r001.rationale: The response describes a discovery loop and choosing experiments, but does not conceptualize research as a tree search.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss scientific papers or describe them as reporting one path through a research search tree.

r003.rationale: It advocates testing systems in experimental environments, but not training on datasets that capture full research search trees.
